title: Refinish or Replace Kitchen Cabinets? How to Decide
description: Refinishing or replacing kitchen cabinets comes down to box condition, layout, and door style. A practical checklist for weighing cost and disruption.
h1: Refinish or Replace Your Cabinets? An Honest Cost Comparison
heroIntro: If the cabinet boxes are solid and the layout works, refinishing usually delivers most of the visual change for far less money and disruption. Here is how to tell which camp your kitchen falls into.
excerpt: Box condition, layout, and door style decide whether to refinish or replace kitchen cabinets. A practical checklist for weighing cost and disruption.

secondary: is it worth painting kitchen cabinets
questions: Is it cheaper to refinish or replace kitchen cabinets?
How do I know if my cabinets are worth refinishing?
How long does cabinet refinishing take compared to replacement?

sections.h2: The real question: what is wrong with the kitchen?
body: People usually start this decision by looking at the finish: dated oak, yellowed white paint, worn edges. But the finish is the easiest part of a cabinet to change. What should drive the decision is everything underneath it: the condition of the boxes, whether the layout works for how you cook, and whether you like the shape of the doors.

If you only dislike the color, refinishing is almost always the better value. If you dislike where things are, how much storage there is, or the construction is falling apart, no amount of paint will fix that. Answering three questions honestly will point you in the right direction.

It also helps to think about timing. If you plan to sell within a few years, a clean, neutral refinish often gives buyers the updated look they want without the expense of a full remodel. If this is your long-term home and the kitchen frustrates you every day, putting the money toward a layout that works may be the better investment, even if it takes longer to save for.
Open every door and drawer and look inside, especially under the sink and next to the dishwasher, where leaks do the most damage.
bullets: Solid wood and plywood boxes in good shape are excellent candidates for refinishing.
Particleboard that has swollen, crumbled, or delaminated from water damage is a reason to replace at least those units.
Face frames should be tight and square, with doors that close evenly.
Drawer boxes that are falling apart can often be replaced individually without replacing the cabinets.
Thermofoil or vinyl-wrapped doors that are peeling are a special case: the wrap usually has to be removed or the doors replaced, since paint does not bond reliably to failing thermofoil.

body: Refinishing keeps every cabinet exactly where it is. That is ideal if the work triangle makes sense, there is enough counter space, and storage is adequate. If you have always wanted an island, a pantry wall, a relocated sink, or taller uppers, you are really planning a remodel, and new cabinets are part of that project.

There is a middle path. Some kitchens keep most of their cabinets and replace one section, add a few new units, or convert an upper to open shelving. When everything is painted together, new and old cabinets blend into one consistent finish.

sections.h2: Question 3: do you like the door style?
body: Paint changes color, not shape. A raised-panel cathedral door will still be a raised-panel cathedral door in white. Many traditional door styles look fresh and even classic once painted, especially with updated hardware. If you strongly dislike the profile, replacing only the doors and drawer fronts while refinishing the boxes is a common compromise. Heavily grained oak is another consideration; our guide on painting oak cabinets explains the extra grain-filling step needed for a smooth look.

Every kitchen is different, so rather than quote numbers, it helps to understand what each option includes. Replacement means removing the old cabinets, often damaging countertops and backsplash in the process, then buying new cabinets, installing them, and frequently replacing countertops, plumbing connections, and flooring where the old footprint does not match. The kitchen is usually unusable for weeks, and lead times on new cabinetry can add more.

Refinishing keeps the countertops, backsplash, plumbing, and appliances in place. The cost is mainly labor for prep and spraying, plus materials. Doors and drawers are typically finished off-site or in a protected area while the boxes are done in place, and the kitchen is usually back in service in days rather than weeks. Factors that affect the price include the number of doors and drawers, the condition of the existing finish, whether the grain needs filling, and any repairs.

sections.h2: Signs that replacement really is the better choice
body: Refinishing is not always the answer, and a good contractor should tell you when it is not. Replacement usually wins when:
bullets: Water damage has swollen or softened the particleboard in several cabinets, not just one sink base.
The cabinets are a low-grade builder line with stapled joints that are already pulling apart.
You plan to move plumbing, appliances, or walls, so the existing cabinets will not fit the new plan anyway.
You want features painted cabinets cannot add, such as deeper drawers, taller uppers, or a different configuration.
Most of the doors are peeling thermofoil, which would need replacing regardless.

body: The durability of painted cabinets depends almost entirely on the process. A proper refinish should include:
bullets: Removing doors, drawers, and hardware, and labelling everything.
Thorough degreasing, because kitchen grease prevents adhesion.
Scuff sanding, repairing dings, and filling old hardware holes if hardware is changing.
A bonding primer suited to the existing finish, plus stain blocking where needed.
Two coats of a cabinet-grade enamel, such as a waterborne urethane enamel, ideally sprayed for a smooth finish.
Adequate cure time before rehanging, then new hinges, soft-close hardware, or pulls if desired.

sections.h2: Making the most of a refinish
body: A few upgrades done at the same time make painted cabinets feel close to new: soft-close hinges and drawer slides, new pulls and knobs, crown molding at the top of the uppers, and under-cabinet lighting. If you are not sure what color will work with your counters and floors, a color consultation helps, and if you already have painted cabinets that are failing, read our guide to peeling cabinet paint first.

faqs.q: Is refinishing cabinets cheaper than replacing them?
faqs.a: In most kitchens, yes, because refinishing keeps the existing boxes, countertops, plumbing, and backsplash in place. Replacement often triggers new countertops and other work. The exact difference depends on the size of the kitchen and the condition of the cabinets.

faqs.q: How long do painted kitchen cabinets last?
faqs.a: With proper degreasing, sanding, bonding primer, and a cabinet-grade enamel, painted cabinets can hold up for many years. Shortcuts in prep are the main reason painted cabinets chip or peel early.

faqs.q: Can I replace only the cabinet doors?
faqs.a: Yes. If the boxes are sound but you dislike the door style, new doors and drawer fronts can be installed and the boxes refinished to match.
Intact thermofoil can sometimes be painted with specialized primers, but peeling thermofoil cannot be painted reliably. Those doors usually need to be stripped of the wrap or replaced.
